reporter: Skip Snow Everglades National Park
Museum: "Florida Museum of Natural History Herpetology Collection                                                                                                                                                                                                       "
Reference: "Skip Snow, National Park Service, personal communication"
Locality: "Everglades National Park, Hammock just N of the park visitor's center"
Comments: "On 17 April 2008 we had a tegu tail captured on a camera trap deployed as part of the park's mammal survey, located just inside the park near the headquarters building. We put a double door trap, designed for monitors, at the site and baited with cat food. We kept a camera at the site, which is a grassy savanna site with scattered pines. No luck, and after awhile the camera was needed elsewhere. The camera was pulled and two days ago the trap was moved about 20 or so meters to the edge of a hammock and baited with cat food. Thanks to the attention of UF mammal tech Jen Eells, a tegu was captured. The trap will be redeployed at the same hammock for awhile. Lee Fitzgerald identified the species as Tupinambis teguixin, native to northern South America. "

reporter: Skip Snow Everglades National Park
Museum: "Florida Museum of Natural History Herpetology Collection                                                                                                                                                                                                       "
Reference: "Skip Snow, National Park Service, personal communication"
Locality: "Key Largo, vicinity of Overseas Highway and Francis Drake Dr"
Comments: "At about 1:10 pm on Tuesday, 24 June 2008, the Python Hotline received a call from Sue Nulman, 98610 Overseas Highway (Bayside) Key Largo. Ms. Nulman had found a python on her property in a shaded area attempting to eat one of her "pet" birds, one of many wild doves (and other wildlife) she feeds. The Nulman property appears to be rather large and wooded. At around 12:30 pm she saw the python, mostly concealed by leaves, with a dove, dead but not swallowed. Nulman stunned the snake with a blow to the head and then severed the spinal cord. I was in the area so stopped to pick up the carcass, and chat. She expressed concern about the remaining wildlife and the dog, and how to secure the house against pythons. Nulman got the Python Hotline number from a flyer she picked up in Big Cypress. I took the carcass back to the lab and performed a necropsy late in the afternoon. Results are as follows: PyMo_901, a male, some rigor in the carcass, 207.5 cm (TL), 181.0 cm (SVL), with a mass of 3.972 kg and a girth of 18.5 cm. Looks to be near mature, perhaps breeding for the first time this coming winter. No external parasites observed. A couple of large round worms were found in the lower gut, which seem to be associated with a large quantity of fecal material (hair observed). Gut contents were collected and frozen. Mike Rochford and I identified two black rats (Rattus rattus) in the remains collected from the lower gut. The stomach was empty, and a very small amount of unidentified material was collected from the esophagus (also frozen). The carcass was retained (frozen) as a specimen for the FLMNH. Photos were taken by me and by Ms. Nulman (she will email her photos). In general, another rather unremarkable young male Burmese python shows up in Paradise. "

Comments: "On 25 September 2009, Ron Rozar, USGS, and crew, caught a Burmese python in a trap on Key Largo. The animal was a male, with a live measured snout-to-vent length of 185 cm, total length of 207 cm, and a mass of 4.014 kg. The animal was caught in an unbaited, round entrance trap located on a drift fence near the western boundary of the Crocodile Lake NWR (~0.33 km NE of the US 1 - CR 905 split). The UTM coordinates of the capture are 563194; 2784405. The body condition of the snake was good, though its disposition left a little to be desired. The animal was necropsied on 28 September. The animal was a male with testes still developing, ducts thin, not thickened, nor convoluted. Stomach was empty. Three small fecal pellets were collected from the lower GI tract. Mike Rochford (UF) and Skip Snow (ENP) confirmed the id of hair, small bone fragments, and a few very small teeth, to be the remains of a black rat (Rattus rattus). Photos were taken and tissue archived (frozen) for genetics, mercury, etc. PyMo_1401. "

reporter: James Duquesnel Monroe County Assistant Land Steward
Locality: "Approach to Old Bahia Honda Bridge, Bahia Honda State Park, 38650 Overseas Highway, Big Pine Key, FL 33043, USA "
Comments: "Removed 200+ green iguanas (80% were sexually mature, and many females were gravid) from Bahia Honda Key between December 2010 and October 2011.  Iguana densities highest south and west of park entrance, especially on or near the fill placed to provide (pre-1929 Labor Day Hurricane) trains with gradual uphill grade for approach to historic Flagler Railroad bridge), though it is likely any iguanas in less used portions of park (esp. north of highway) are more wary and harder to census.  Higher densities here appear to result from combination of three factors: 1) proximity to primary parking area (where pet owners drop off unwanted iguanas), 2) filled bridge approach provides suitable substrate for burrows used as refuge from cold weather, and 3) habituation of iguanas to humans (tourists) who either do no look for/notice iguanas or, who if they do see iguanas, are almost always non-threatening. This last factor makes many of Bahia Honda's iguanas "naive" (easy to observe, approach closely, or even capture), at least in areas heavily used by park visitors."
Reviewer: Larry Connor, FWCC

Comments: "On 29 August 2011 at 0951 Skip Snow examined the carcass of a male (originally reported as a female) P. sebae (PySe_2017) located at the corner of SW 167ave and SW 64 street (UTM 17R 553885; 2843173. The head and a portion of the tail were missing, and the carcass was badly bloated. The total length of the remaining carcass was 317 cm. The animal had been run over by farm machinery apparently clearing trash from the adjacent field (perhaps in preparation for cultivation) probably sometime Friday the 26th, or maybe Saturday the 27th. The python had severe internal trauma between and including the heart and the stomach, but no obvious external lacerations or punctures. It appears the animal was run over perhaps by a tracked vehicle like a small dozer. Prey remains were recovered from the stomach (possible cat) and remains of an older meal were recovered from the lower GI. Both testes were flaccid, not at all swollen nor turgid. A portion of the remaining tail was collected and frozen for genetics, etc. A photo is attached. More photos are available from MDFR. "
Reviewer: Larry Connor, FWCC

Reference: "James G. Duquesnel, U. S. Geological Survey, personal communication"
Locality: "Key Largo, 385 Pompano Dr"
Comments: "Captured behind storm shutter outside second story window on north wall of a three-story private residence. Today gecko heard outside kitchen window was found today and captured with a string noose. The past 8 months, we have noted a significant increase in the number of Tokay geckos that we can hear vocalizing in undeveloped lots of our neighborhood (Anglers Park Subdivision, Mile Marker 103.6 oceanside, Key Largo, Monroe County, Florida). Of those I have tried to find, most appear to be hiding in hollows or under loose slabs of bark at heights above 15 feet in larger trees, usually wild tamarind (Lysiloma latisiliqua), West Indian tamarind (Sweitenia mahagoni), and strangler fig (Ficus aurea). The one I caught today was hiding behind a storm shutter on an outer wall of the second story (of three), approximately 15 feet above grade and on the north (cooler) side of house. I believe it is one that spent the summer calling from a Ficus tree on our lot. "
Reviewer: Larry Connor, FWCC

Comments: "I had never seen anything like this before! I told a friend who showed me a photo of the Nile Monitor lizard online and I recognized it immediately. This one looked like it had algae on it. I watched it from the rear of my home. We have several alligators in the lake and alot of wildlife as it is a wildlife preserve (Eagle Marsh Golf Course in Jensen Beach). I am concerned about swimming in the community pools as they have no screen protection as well as concern for the golfers who may be unaware of what they are dealing with (just did the research on these creatures) I hope this helps and I wonder if there is anything that can be done about this? I was not able to photograph it in time as I had no idea what I was dealing with until later. Larry Connor, FWCC, contacted the reporter and sent photos of several lizards. Comments: "I heard a flapping of metal outside my window, and went out to see if the lawnmower had caught something in the blades (someone was cutting my fields). The noise was very loud, and I ran to see if an accident had occured. When I went out onto the porch, I notice the noise was coming from the air conditioner. I ran over, and saw the fan cutting something, blood and meat coming through the grate on top. I saw a long, black tail about 1 foot long above the revolving fan. I could not see a body or anything, but after the fan stopped, I looked closer and saw pieces of feet and legs stuck in the grating. The coloring is like the B&W Tegu, and the feet and claws look the same. I tried to look down in the ac unit, but have not been able to see anything. I did see where the compressor wrapping has been knocked off. I am going out of town, but my brother will be at my home, and I would like someone to come see if the thing is a Tegu. I have never seen any lizard or anything resembling the body pieces in my yard or fields since I have lived here for over 6 years. I have dogs and cats and am concerned. Please contact me, and, hopefully someon can come and see what it is. I will ask my brother not to take the air conditioner grates off until I hear from someone, or get back home on Friday. The airconditioner is next to the house. Please come check this out. Airconditiioning repair technician inspected the unit, but did not recover or photograph the carcass. "

reporter: James Duquesnel Monroe County Assistant Land Steward
Museum: "Florida Museum of Natural History Herpetology Collection                                                                                                                                                                                                       "
Reference: "James G. Duquesnel, U. S. Geological Survey, personal communication"
Locality: "Key Largo, Pompano Ave appx 280 m W of US-1"
Comments: "This python was first observed moving from south to north across Pompano Avenue, a paved street in a relatively quiet neighborhood - the Bowens Addition to Riviera Village subdivision on Key Largo, approximately 300 meters west (bayside) of U.S. Highway Route 1 (a.k.a. State Road 5) mile marker 105. It moved off the cleared right-of-way, and into cover just inside the margin of hardwood hammock at Block 6, Lots 16, 17 and 18 of Bowens Addition to Riviera Village Subdivision. As a former resident of 38 Pompano Avenue (100 feet from where the snake was observed), I would describe this subdivision as heavily wooded despite being 75% developed, and much less than 75% occupied during August, as many residents leave for the summer. Most of the properties at the west end of the subdivision (west of Bay Drive and on Blackwater Sound) are large and many retain remnants of hardwood hammock. Between Bay Drive and US Route 1, many of the homeowners have retained at least large shade trees, some have kept small remnants of the native forest. There are also many undeveloped lots still covered by dense hardwood hammock, with vines and poisonwood (Metopium toxiferum) often making access less than convenient. Any constrictor, as long as it remained undetected by residents, would find ample prey here as there are many free-roaming domestic cats, as well as resident opossums, raccoons, grey squirrels, and abundant non-native rats (Rattus rattus).  On 30-August-2012, at approximately 11:00 PM, Monroe County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) Deputy Bryan Cross was conducting routine patrols of Key Largo's residential neighborhoods when he observed a large snake moving from south to north across a Monroe County right-of-way. Estimating the snake's length at 10 feet, Deputy Cross called Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) dispatch for assistance. Responding FWC Officers Jason Rafter, Kip Hoover and Shelton Bartlet were joined by MCSO Sergeant Jason Madnick, and the five officers searched the area until finding the python, at about 11:25 PM, under a brush pile just inside the hardwood hammock of undeveloped lots (across from # 32 Pompano Avenue, Key Largo, FL 33037) and just a few yards from where it had been first observed. The following afternoon (31-Aug-2012), Officer Rafter transferred the live python to United States Geological Survey (USGS) Invasive Species Science biologists James Duquesnel and Michelle McEachern. During the transfer, Duquesnel took several photos (three are attached to this report) of the snake and Officers Rafter and Hoover, assisted by FWC Officer Janet Fernandez, who helped hold the snake for the photo. McEachern then transported the snake to Everglades National Park's Dan Beard Center, where Wildlife Biologist Skip Snow confirmed the species identification, and reported the following after his post-mortem examination: mass: 9,448 grams; snout to vent length: 254 cm; total length: 287 cm (9 ft., 4 in.); girth: 25.4 cm. Both ovaries with numerous small follicles (max dia. 8.0 mm, 7.2, 6.9) Oviducts thin and narrow, not at all thick nor muscular. Virgin female. Stomach empty. Moderate amount of fecal material collected from lower GI (frozen), hair observed and numerous large parasitic worms (70% ETOH). Tail collected (frozen) A few mites and one lungworm also collected (70% ETOH) Carcass retained for FLMNH (frozen). AVID scan negative. Body with a few small old scars. The specimen will most likely be deposited in the collection at Florida Museum of Natural History (Gainesville, FL). "
Reviewer: Larry Connor, FWCc

reporter: James Duquesnel Monroe County Assistant Land Steward
Reference: "James G. Duquesnel, U. S. Geological Survey, personal communication"
Locality: "Miami-Dade County, SW 424th St appx 280 m W of US-1"
Comments: "Driving west on SW 424th Street, I observed a small black and white tegu standing two feet north of the paved surface, facing traffic, and roughly 10 feet away from a road-killed armadillo carcass. Before I could get camera out, the tegu retreated into vegetation. However, this was the smallest tegu of approx. 25 I have seen free-roaming; I would estimate weight at 0.5 kg. Just 3 to 4 meters away was an armadillo carcass, though it appeared to have been cleaned out fairly well by scavengers, fire ants and the elements. I also noticed several lubber grasshoppers crossing the road in the vicinity, easy prey... if a tegu did not find the noxious taste a deterrent. "
Reviewer: Larry Connor, FWCC

reporter: James Duquesnel Monroe County Assistant Land Steward

Reference: "James G. Duquesnel, U. S. Geological Survey, personal communication"
Locality: "Key Largo, vicinity of Mahogany Dr and US-1"
Comments: "As community made preparations for potential landfall of Tropical Storm Isaac, I was contacted by the owner of a private residence on Mahogany Drive, Key Largo, FL. At the site, I found tokay geckos ranging from newly hatched to large adults. I collected four using either gloved hand (for two smallest) or a noose pole (for larger specimens). After dark, tokay geckos were visible all over the outside of this residence; I estimate that I observed at least 12 in the 15 minutes I was there. I also photographed a large mass of eggs that were attached to the wall where storm shutters had been stored (see attached images). This species has been increasing rapidly in Key Largo; now I understand why. "
Reviewer: Larry Connor, FWCC

Comments: "The Florida Keys Free Press published a photo and caption under the headline "Another Python" on page 8 of the paper's October 3, 2012 edition. When I reported this record to EDDMaps, the photo and caption were available online at: http://pdf.keysnews.com/weeklys/freepress.pdf Just in case that is no longer the case: The photo shows a man holding the snake by its tail. The man (approximately 5'9" tall, according to Ms. Dillon) has his arm extended upwards at a 45 degree angle, and the snake's head does not quite reach the ground The published estimated length of "almost seven feet" appears reasonable. Below the photo is the following caption: "Key Largo resident Beverly Dillon found an almost 7-foot python in front of her house Thursday, Sept. 28, after workers began clearing a lot across the street from her South Ocean Shores home. 'This great big thing crawled right in front of the street,' Dillon said. ‘It was fighting and going nuts.' The workers killed the invasive snake. Officials are beginning to find more and more pythons coming south from Everglades National Park." My October 6 telephone call to the witness cited in the caption (Beverly Dillon) produced additional details. The snake was discovered during routine maintenance / clearing of brush on an overgrown vacant lot on South Ocean Shores Drive, Key Largo, Florida. Employees of the landscape maintenance company killed the python, and took the the carcass away when they left, as requested by residents of the adjacent property. Ms. Dillon also mentioned that residents of another home in the neighborhood reportedly own and breed pythons. The location information is intentionally vague as I am not sure if the snake was on the County-owned right-of-way or the adjacent privately-owned vacant lot. It was on the half of South Ocean Shores Drive that is west of Ocean Bay Drive, Key Largo, Florida. The owner of the adjacent private lot was not contacted regarding this report, so the location given is intentionally imprecise, and is shown as intersection of South Ocean Shores Drive and Ocean Bay Drive (accurate within 300 meters).  Larry Connor, FWCC, changed the observation date to 9/27/2012 based on image properties of the iPhone image provided by Beverly Dillon. "
Reviewer: Larry Connor, FWCC

Comments: "Gravid female boa captured at Key West International Airport by Monroe County Sheriff's Office personnel. Snake was also reported on EDDMapS. The Key West Citizen (http://keysnews.com/node/42846) and Florida Keys Keynoter (http://www.keysnet.com/2012/10/12/482726/10-foot-python-found-at-key-west.html) newspapers reported that a large constrictor at the Key West Airport on Thursday, October 11, 2012. I have requested permission to attach (to this report) photos taken by Monroe County Sheriff's Office Sergeant Evan Calhoun; two were published (one in each) of the local newspapers cited in this record. The Key West Citizen published the snake's correct identification in a story by staff writer Adam Linhardt. The following is an excerpt from Linhardt's article as posted October 13 (2012) at http://keysnews.com/node/42846: A 10-foot boa constrictor captured by deputies and Key West International Airport authorities Thursday night most likely is a released or escaped pet and did not make its way to Key West from the Florida Everglades, officials said Friday. "This is a large red-tailed boa," Marathon veterinarian Doug Mader said Friday in an email to The Citizen. "It looks, in the photo, very healthy, so I suspect it is eating plenty." The boa constrictor was found at 6:30 p.m., right behind the terminal near a grassy area, said Monroe County Airports Director Peter Horton. Airport authorities turned the snake over to Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) officers, Horton said." The Keynoter article (incorrectly) reported, both online and in their paper edition, that the snake was a python: "A 10-foot python -- a nonnative invasive species -- was found in the grass near the edge of the commercial ramp at Key West International Airport Thursday." As I post this report, I have not yet learned who has the snake, though newspapers reported that it was turned over to FWC officers (James G. Duquesnel, U. S. Geological Survey, personal communication). "

Locality: "Manatee County, I-275 under bridge appx 475 m E of US-41"
Comments: "Ctenosaura pectinata was found on a rocky enbankment along a canal underneath the I-275 bridge. There are several rocks and areas to provide cover for more iguanas. My friend Greg Hebert saw an iguana basking on a rock. As the iguana went for cover in the rocks, Greg was able to grab its tail. The female is roughly 2 feet long. Another lizard was seen but was able to escape. That species could not be identified. The image was reviewed by Dr. Kenney Krysko, FLMNH, Kevin Enge, FWCC, and Dr. John Himes, FWCC. The lizard identified as most likely C. pectinata with an unusual color pattern pending additional photographs or specimens. "
Reviewer: Larry Connor, FWCC
ReviewComm: "Photo reviewed by Dr. Kenney Krysko, FLMNH, Dr. John Himes, FWCC, and Kevin Enge, FWCC. Concensus was that it was most likely a C. pectinata, but based on the unusual color pattern could be another species. I marked it as a verified C. pectinata pending more photographs and/or specimen."

reporter: James Duquesnel Monroe County Assistant Land Steward
Museum: "Florida Museum of Natural History Herpetology Collection                                                                                                                                                                                                       "
Reference: "James G. Duquesnel, U. S. Geological Survey, personal communication"
Locality: "Crocodile Lake National Wildlife Refuge, headquarters buildings CR-905 and Ocean Dr"
Comments: "On the 180-degree bend of a wheelchair access ramp, at southwest corner of Crocodile Lake Wildlife Refuge office building (a double-wide trailer elevated approximately two feet above grade). A dense planting of golden beach creeper (Ernodea littoralis) and a deep accumulation of leaf-litter under the ramp and elevated building create ample cover. The property also has poured concrete pad: ADA parking space, and a concrete pad under the air-conditioner unit, providing just the type of solid cover under which Leiocephalus seems to prefer to burrow as well as a constant supply of dripping fresh water (condensate draining onto the concrete pad from the air conditioner). Two northern curly-tailed lizards (Leicephalus carinatus armouri) were observed on August 28; neither as large as they grow, though both looked large enough to reproduce. Refuge Manager Jeremy Dixon got to see the smaller one basking on the ramp's raised decking, just before it hid. Walking behind the building for another view, we found a second slightly larger Leiocephalus running toward the location of the first across the back of the building. I retrieved my camera from the car, but a black racer (charcoal gray Upper Keys color form) showed up and the lizards remained hidden. The place was and (as of Sep 13) is swarming with very small to full-sized Anolis sagrei. Despite efforts by several people, Leiocephalus were not seen at that location again until I got photos of the larger one on September 12, within a meter of where we lost sight of it on August 28. Approximately September 5, Dixon saw what may have been a third Leiocephalus just 35 meters north of the other sightings, midway along the back fence of CLWR's storage yard. He also had another sighting in front (east) of the office, very close to where the first two were seen. "
Reviewer: Larry Connor, FWCC

Comments: "Observation of what seemed likely to be a Burmese python was found in search of MCSO Dispatcher's Logs: Saturday. February 6. 2010 15:25 COWART, RYAN 9182 MCS010CAD013751 1 MARLIN AVE SOUTH KEY LARGO, MARLIN AVE SOUTH 103.4 OC - SYLVESTRI, JR. (305) 522-2385 I interviewed Joseph R Silvestri on 23 Sep 2013. A home construction contractor, Silvestri lives on SE Marlin Avenue, in Largo Sound Park subdivision (mile marker 103.3). Leaving home to go to a worksite, he noticed a crowd gathering at a new residence he was building at #1 SE Marlin Avenue. Stopping, he asked why they were on his lot, and was told some of them has watched a very large snake disappear into a pile of boulders he had on the site. Using a backhoe he had parked there, he removed boulders from the pile until he saw enough of the snake to identifiy it as a python. He then called the MCSO non-emergency line to report it, and waited until FWC officers arrived and captured the python. FWC officers told Silvestri privately that they would euthanize the snake once they had it away from the public eye. The snake was not measured before it was taken away, but Silvestri said that an article in a local paper the following week mentioned that the snake was a 9 feet 6 inches long Burmese python. One of the officers says the snake is 8'10" in the video (Larry Connor, FWCC, personal communication). See this photo voucher (video) on YouTube: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=snbXJOG1h0U "

reporter: James Duquesnel Monroe County Assistant Land Steward
Museum: "Florida Museum of Natural History Herpetology Collection                                                                                                                                                                                                       "
Reference: "James G. Duquesnel, U. S. Geological Survey, personal communication"
Locality: "Key Largo, Fishermans Trl 100 m S of US-1"
Comments: "County right-of-way (Blue Runner) southeast of US Route 1 (Overseas Highway) approximately Mile Marker 99.1 oceanside, 100 feet east of Fisherman's Trail. The same tegu (apparently) escaped from its owner at 106 Ocean Drive, and was subsequently photographed (and reported to FWC) at 104 Ocean Shores Drive near Fisherman's Trail on October 10 (see EDDMapS Record 3066707), at 102 Ocean Shores Drive and on Fisherman's Trail on October 11, and on Fisherman's Trail near US Route 1 on October 13. I began setting egg-baited live-traps (borrowed from Croc Lake WR) and distributing and posting leaflets with a photo of a tegu and IVE-GOT-1 contact info throughout the neighborhood starting Oct 11. A homeowner on Blue Runner near mile marker 99 on Key Largo (FL) called Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) to report an unusual lizard in her yard. The description she provided matched that of an Argentine black and white tegu (Salvator merianae) that had been reported to EDDMapS on October 11, 2013. I was dispatched to the address and caller pointed out a tegu basking in pea-rock (white limestone gravel) at the edge of rockland hammock. As capture equipment was being readied, the tegu began to leave, calling for faster action. It was approached and, using leather gloves, captured by hand after a brief display of hissing, arched back, slow-tail lashing and a weak lunge at my approaching hand; this was the "softest" (least muscular) tegu I have ever handled. It was turned over to FWC the following day."
Reviewer: Larry Connor, FWCC

reporter: Lauren Pelak Self-employed
Reference: "Personal Communication"
Locality: "Naples, parking lot Berkshire Commons"
Comments: "Saw a large green lizard sunning himself in the parkinglot. He wasn't traditional iguana but he had large claws. His eyes were very round and large. I would not have even noticed him at all but he charged at me. I have owned reptiles as pets before but this lizard was aggressive! I tried looking him up online and I suspect he may be a Cuban Knight Anole but I don't know much about them. I could tell whatever he is, he was not fully grown. His coloring didn't match pictures of any of the adult invasives I looked up online. It concerns me because a friend of mine gave an identical description of this type of lizard in Cambier Park in Naples two days after I saw one. (And Cambier Park is a good 5 miles from where I saw this one!) I did not think to grab a picture but she did take a picture and it is the exact same type of lizard.
